When something is strenuous, it demands a great deal of physical or mental energy and effort. It pushes you, tires you out, and requires you to work hard. Think of it as the opposite of easy or relaxed.

If a task is strenuous, it is not merely difficult in a puzzle-like way — it is actively draining. It takes real force out of you.
The Two Main Ways It Is Used

1. Describing an activity or task

This is the most common use. Here, "strenuous" describes something you do that is physically or mentally demanding and exhausting.

  • Climbing a steep mountain is a strenuous activity.
  • Running a marathon is strenuous exercise.
  • Working 14-hour shifts in a factory is strenuous labor.
  • Studying advanced mathematics for 8 hours straight is strenuous mental work.

In all these cases, you come away from the activity feeling genuinely worn out — because you gave it a lot of energy.

2. Describing an effort, attempt, or action

Here, "strenuous" describes how hard or forcefully someone tries to do something — including arguing, objecting, or defending a position. In this sense, it means vigorous and intense.

  • The lawyer made a strenuous effort to win the case.
  • She raised a strenuous objection to the plan.
  • He made a strenuous attempt to save the drowning child.
  • The team put up a strenuous defense.

In this use, "strenuous" is about the intensity of will and action behind something — not just physical tiredness, but the forcefulness of a push or a fight.

What makes "strenuous" special — and different from just saying hard or difficult — is that it always carries the idea of active, energetic exertion. It is not passive difficulty. Something strenuous demands that you put in real, vigorous work.

Think of it this way:

  • A complicated puzzle might be difficult, but sitting quietly and thinking about it is not strenuous.
  • Digging a ditch in the summer heat is strenuous — because your whole body is exerting force, and you are being worn down.

So "strenuous" is specifically about the expenditure of energy and effort — it has a sense of sweat, strain, and push behind it.

When you call something strenuous, you are also subtly saying:

  • It is not for everyone. It requires ability, strength, or endurance.
  • It will tire you. Rest may be needed afterward.
  • It demands commitment. You cannot do it halfheartedly.

The word is not necessarily negative, though. A strenuous workout is tough, but many people seek it out intentionally. A strenuous effort to save someone is admirable. The word simply highlights the level of energy required or given.

• "Doctors advised him to avoid strenuous activity after his heart surgery."
  • "She made a strenuous effort to finish the project before the deadline."
  • "Hiking with a heavy backpack is far more strenuous than a gentle walk in the park."
  • "The union leaders mounted a strenuous opposition to the new working conditions."
  • "Even though she was tired, she made one last strenuous push to reach the summit."

These words share the general idea of being demanding or exhausting:

  • Arduous — very hard and tiring, often over a long period (climbing a mountain is arduous).
  • Vigorous — done with strong, active energy (a vigorous run).
  • Exhausting — leaves you with no energy left.
  • Demanding — requires a lot from you.
  • Taxing — drains your energy or patience.

"Strenuous" sits right in the middle of this family — it emphasizes both the effort required and the vigor of the action.

• Easy, effortless, light, gentle, relaxing, leisurely.

A leisurely walk is the opposite of a strenuous hike.

Strenuous means requiring or involving great, active, and vigorous effort — the kind that pushes you hard and leaves you tired. Whether describing a grueling task or a powerful attempt, it always signals that significant energy is at work.
